author: opt-B1

contract.sync_assumed: caller separates consecutive calls that reuse the temp storage by a block barrier
contract.sync_performed: __syncthreads inside: 1 after the bracket reduction (shared with the histogram zeroing), 2 per pass (1 to 3 fixed-point passes, then key passes over the candidates on the exact fallback), none in the epilogue
contract.n_range: N = 256 x IPT, IPT >= 1, measured 1024 to 32768, temp storage independent of N
contract.type_constraints: fp32 and bf16 (bf16 widened to fp32 once in the prologue), int32 indices derived from the striped tile position
contract.nan_behavior: NaN not supported (never produced by focus-set inputs). Infinities clamp into the end bins of the fixed-point image and are ordered exactly by the key passes if the pivot falls on them. -0.0 and +0.0 share one image, they form one tie class only under prefer_smaller_index where the prologue folds -0.0 onto +0.0
contract.tie_break_support: ticket order under not_guaranteed, warp-redundant rank under prefer_smaller_index (IPT at most 64), as B1_det
contract.sorted_output_support: not supported inherently, post-sort of k

correctness_notes: 22 cells, 13 oracle cases each, all passed in this batch. The previous build of the same source failed the inf_denorm pattern in the 4 cells with k 1024 (full bracket [-inf, +inf] clamped to [-FLT_MAX, FLT_MAX], whose width overflows fp32 and made the scale 0, so that -inf times 0 gave NaN and -inf landed in a top bin): the scale is now finite and nonzero in every case and the image is clamped on both sides. That batch (n6a) is kept under state/results/opt-B1 for its 36 valid cells and is not a card.

low_level: Per item per pass the fixed-point digit costs FADD, FFMA (with the 2^23 rounding constant), two IMNMX (clamps), LOP3 and ISETP (prefix filter), SHF and LOP3 (digit and bucket flip) before the ATOMS, against LOP3, ISETP, SHF, LOP3 for the radix digit: about 4 instructions more per item per pass. The bracket costs one FMNMX pair per item (per-thread max and min), three redux.sync (T1) and lane 0 stores per warp, and 24 shared loads plus 14 min or max per thread after the barrier that the histogram zeroing needs anyway: no extra barrier.

This build kept one fixed-point image per item live across the passes (the compiler hoisted the loop-invariant FADD and FFMA out of the pass sequence): 40 registers at IPT 4 against 32 for B1_idx, 80 against 47 at IPT 16 (occupancy 3 against 4 blocks per SM in throughput), 255 with 8572 to 8588 bytes of spill against 250 with 0 at IPT 128, where the spill dominates the result (30398 against 16464 cycles at bf16 N 32768 k 16). The previous build of the same algorithm (n6a, before the clamp and scale changes) spilled 1464 to 1508 bytes and measured 11983 at that cell, 27 percent faster than B1_idx: the per-pass recompute is a codegen lottery, which the next variant pins with an opaque per-pass copy of the bracket parameters.

Tie-class tracking in this build takes the min and max over all candidates of the pass, not over the pivot bucket, so a bf16 tie class inside a larger candidate set is detected one pass late: bf16 at N 1024 k 64 and 256 runs 3 fixed-point passes where 2 would do (2213 against 1877 and 2681 against 1971 for B1_idx's 2 radix passes).
algorithmic: Where the bracket pass replaces two radix passes by one (small k, the pivot bucket holds exactly the remaining k or a single value), N6 wins: N 1024 k 16 bf16 1700 against 1768, fp32 1673 against 1794, N 4096 k 16 bf16 2846 against 3369 (16 percent), fp32 2887 against 3663 (21 percent), fp32 N 4096 k 64 3906 against 4585, k 256 4607 against 5047, N 32768 k 16 fp32 14210 against 15154 despite 8.6 KB of spill. The host simulation (sim_passes.md section 2) predicted the pivot bin after one pass at 1.1 to 7.3 items (mean, at most 16) for every random cell with k at most 256 under the thread-max bracket, and the exact exit after the second pass in 97 to 100 percent of the rows, which the GPU confirms where the register footprint does not intervene.

Where ties at the k-th key need the tie-class exit (bf16, 1.4 to 54 ties at rank k) the late detection of this build costs a pass and N6 loses at k 64 and above (bf16 N 1024 k 256 2681 against 1971, N 4096 k 256 5570 against 4513). fp32 at k 256 is within 5 percent at N 1024 and 9 percent ahead at N 4096.

The kill criteria of the idea card: (1) one pass plus a finish on at least 90 percent of random and logit-like rows holds in the host simulation for every k at most 256 (100 percent of rows end with at most 16 items in the pivot bin, 97 to 100 percent are exact after the second pass), and fails for k above 256 without a tighter lower bound (217 items in the pivot bin at N 32768 k 4096). (2) the per-item cost of the bin function is about 4 instructions per item per pass over the radix extractor, under 10 percent of a pass at IPT 4 (the pass is dependency bound) and about 7 percent of the histogram sweep at IPT 128. N6 is not killed, its gain is real at small k and at fp32, and its weak spots (late tie exit, register footprint) are implementation, not idea.
negative: Tracking the key min and max over all candidates of a pass (two atomics on two words) is not enough to exit on a bf16 tie class: the pivot bucket of pass p is a tie class long before the whole candidate set is, so bf16 paid a third pass at k 64 and 256 in every N.

Recomputing the fixed-point image per pass from the fp32 value is only cheap if the compiler does recompute it. Left to itself it keeps IPT images live across the passes, which costs 8 registers per item at IPT 4 and 8.6 KB of spill at IPT 128.
surprises: One extra IMNMX per item (the upper clamp added for +inf) and a changed scale expression moved the kernel from 1464 to 8588 bytes of spill at IPT 128 and from 64 to 80 registers at IPT 16, with the algorithm unchanged: the compiler's decision to hoist the image across the passes flipped. The 2.5x swing at N 32768 between the two builds of the same algorithm is the largest codegen effect seen in this study so far.

The inf_denorm battery pattern caught the degenerate bracket: hi equal to plus infinity and lo to minus infinity give a width that overflows fp32, a zero scale and NaN images for the infinite items. The clamps and the finite nonzero scale cost one instruction per item per pass.
open_questions: With per-bucket tracking (next variant) does bf16 reach the predicted one-pass exit at N 4096 and 32768 (the simulation says the pivot bin is a single bf16 value in 100 percent of the rows there for k at most 256)? The first pass does not track, so that exit still needs a representable-value test on the pivot bin's value interval, cheap and block-uniform, not yet written.

A tighter lower bound for k above 256 (the minimum over threads of the per-thread second or m-th largest, B4's bound) would extend the one-pass regime to k 256 m, the full bracket leaves 37 to 217 items in the pivot bin at k 1024 and 4096.
